lede: Liturgy & Chanting · บทสวด accounts for 97 catalogued manuscripts, 6 of them flagged research-priority. It clusters in Phrae (22% of the corpus for this genre), ahead of Lampang and Nan. Nearly all (94%) are written in Tham Lanna · อักษรธรรมล้านนา script. By support it leans to palm-leaf · ใบลาน (69%) over mulberry paper (saa) · กระดาษสา (29%). Dated witnesses run 1541–1964 CE (56 of 97 carry a date).

authored.title: Liturgy & Chanting
authored.body_html:
What this is

This is the performed end of the Buddhist corpus — not scripture to be studied but words to be said aloud, in a room, at an hour, by a named number of monks. The catalogue files all 97 witnesses as Chanting, and the titles lay out the northern liturgical repertoire almost as a working diary of the year: the fortnightly sut mon, the thon recited over a bad death, the suat boek that opens a rite, the invitation that summons a preacher to begin the Vessantara.

The technology is the same as the katha's — a formula said aloud to make something happen — and the difference from saiyasat is not the mechanism. It is the audience.

What gets chanted, and why — the origin stories

The chants of the paritta set are not abstract protections. Each one carries a story explaining what it once saved, and Supreme Maha Mantra Katha — a contributed printed volume with full transcription and translation — sets them out one after another. Read three of them and the whole logic of protective chanting becomes obvious.

The Karaniya Metta Sutta (p.103) begins as a haunting. Monks take leave of the Buddha to spend the rains retreat in a forest. The rukkha-devatā, the tree spirits, come down to the ground to pay their respects, assuming the visit will be brief. It is not brief. Living on the ground becomes inconvenient, and since they cannot move higher, they resort to frightening the monks out. The monks retreat to the Buddha, who does not exorcise anything; he sends them back with a chant of loving-kindness, and when the devas hear it, loving-kindness arises in them and the haunting stops. Inference — this is the founding case of the whole northern protective repertoire, and it is a negotiation, not an expulsion. The problem is a housing dispute; the solution is good manners addressed to the party with the grievance. Set it beside the mae sü courtesy in the amulet manuals and the same etiquette is running in both.

The Mora Paritta (p.104) is a Bodhisatta-as-golden-peacock story with an unusually harsh ending. The peacock recites the chant morning and evening before going out to feed, and a hunter lies in wait for him for seven years without ever taking him. Then a second hunter changes tactics: he brings a hen peacock as a lure, the peacock is so distracted he forgets to recite — and is caught at once. The protection never failed. The reciter did.

The Vaṭṭaka Paritta (p.105), the "quail chant," is the shortest and the best. A forest fire is running; every animal flees, including the little quail's parents; the fire is about to reach the nest. The chick cannot fly and cannot walk, so it makes a sacca-adhiṭṭhāna, an asseveration of truth, and what it says is simply the truth of its own helplessness: I have wings but cannot fly, I have feet but cannot walk; my parents have fled. Let the flames retreat. They retreat. The words that became the fire-protection chant are a statement of total inability — which is a strange and rather beautiful thing for a power-formula to be made of.

Alongside these the same volume records the practical end of the repertoire — the Aṅgulimāla Paritta recited over water for a woman in labour, or by the labouring woman herself, so that she may give birth easily (p.105); the Bojjhaṅga Paritta, chanted to a sick man who recovers at that very moment (p.105); the Jinapañjara, which invites the 28 Buddhas and the eighty great disciples to take up residence in the reciter's own body and stand around him (p.104); the Khandha Paritta, which protects against venomous creatures by spreading loving-kindness to venomous creatures. And it answers the layperson's question directly, in a section titled What Is Chanting For? (p.110–111), where the compiler simply narrates her own life: chanting before bed as a child in imitation of her grandfather; later, in the capital, with problems she had nowhere to take, chanting as the one thing to hold onto; the Jinapañjara learnt by heart and carried on every journey; ordination as a mae chi, twice; morning chanting and an hour of sitting, every day, for almost ten years. Her theory of the practice is unsentimental — chanting is samatha, an anchor for the mind in one place, a way of fully recharging so it can rise into vipassanā; and if you occasionally chant it wrong, there is no need to worry.

The Uppatasanti — Lanna's own great chant

One text in the corpus is described in the treatises as specifically and anciently northern. The Uppatasanti (อุปปาทสันติ), which Supreme Maha Mantra Katha (p.102) says "has been widely known among the Lanna people since ancient times, called the Great Santing Luang," is a 271-verse roll-call of virtue: 28 Buddhas of the past, one of the future, the Pacceka Buddhas, the nine supramundane states, 108 senior elders and then thirteen more, the nāga kings, certain classes of hungry ghost, the asuras, forty-one verses of devas, sixteen of brahmās, and at the end ten verses on the pacification of calamity itself. It is recited to invoke good fortune, drive off evil, overpower an enemy's strength, guard against non-human beings, and — the phrase is worth keeping — as a Dhamma to escape death before its appointed time.

The catalogue holds five witnesses, and where they are filed is the finding. Two are here under liturgy's neighbours — ms 3124 (Wat Phra That Chang Kham, palm-leaf, 1927) and ms 3125 (Wat Na Pang) under magic and ritual; ms 2560 (Wat Sung Men, palm-leaf, 1767) and ms 3127 (Wat Muang Tuet, 1925) under astrology; ms 3126 (Wat Hia, 1903) under Buddhist canonical. Inference — one text, five copies, four different genre labels. The taxonomy is not failing; the text genuinely is a canonical recitation, a protective working, and a calendrical instrument at once, and each cataloguer filed the face they saw.

The Mahāsamaya Sutta does the same trick at larger scale — 16 witnesses across the corpus, five of them in this genre, the rest mostly canonical. The treatise's own gloss (p.102) explains why a sutta that is simply a very long list of arriving devas became a favourite performance piece: when this text is recited, the devas are pleased to listen because each of them is named. It is a chant that works by roll-call, and the guest list is the point. See Mahāsamaya.

The funeral, counted out in monks

The clearest picture of a northern liturgy in operation comes from Setting Up Ceremonies, Ancient Edition, which sorts every ceremony into two classes on its first working page (p.3): mangala, the auspicious, and the inauspicious — and then gives each its own physics.

The sacred thread runs in opposite directions (p.5). For an auspicious rite, the sai sin begins at the Buddha image or the household shrine, loops clockwise around the building and the ceremony ground, returns to circle the image's base once or three times, and its coil is laid on a tray to the left of the altar. For an inauspicious rite, the thread runs from the corpse — or from the urn of ashes, or from the portrait of the deceased, or from the written list of the dead's names — directly to the monks, for the bangsukul. Inference — the same physical cord is the instrument in both cases; what changes is which end of it a body is attached to.

And the monks are counted (p.6). Ten for a royal or government auspicious rite; five for any ceremony held by the general public, weddings included. For a funeral, royal and commoner alike:

  • 4 monks to chant the Abhidhamma
  • 4 monks to chant before the cremation fire
  • 5, 7, 9 or 10 to chant the blessing texts, according to one's faith
  • 20, 25, 50, 100 or 500 — or the entire monastery — for the sawotchaeng
  • and for the mātikā-bangsukul, a number of monks equal to the age of the deceased

That last line is the one to carry away. A life is converted directly into a quantity of recitation. Tradition holds — the Abhidhamma at a Thai funeral is famously not chanted for the mourners' comprehension; the seven books are recited as the densest available concentration of Dhamma, offered on behalf of the dead, and the north's mātikā — the bare list of Abhidhamma headings — is the version most often heard over a coffin. The archive's palm-leaf shelf carries the northern verses that go with it: ms 432 at Wat Hia includes คำไหว้อภิธัมมาเจ็ดกัมพี, the words of homage to the seven books of the Abhidhamma, bound beside a meditation manual and a Buddha-veneration text.

The same treatise then descends, without changing tone, into modern administration (p.147): report a death at a hospital and collect the medical certificate; report a death at home to the registrar, the sub-district doctor, the headman or the kamnan within 24 hours; in an accident or a homicide, call the police and do not move the body. The ceremonial handbook and the civil registry are the same book.

The shape of the collection

Liturgy is written overwhelmingly in Tham Lanna — 91 of 97 — but its language profile is the most distinctive in the archive: 15 witnesses are monolingual Pali, needing no vernacular at all, because the chant is the Pali and a reciter who has the melody does not need a gloss. Three are Pali and Lao in Tham Lao script, all from Wat Sung Men and all dated 1836; three are Pali and Shan, including ms 4437 at Wat Pa Pao in Chiang Mai (khoi paper, 1916) and two at Wat Si Khom Kham in Phayao. For a genre of 97, that is four liturgical languages sharing one shelf.

Its support leans harder to paper (28 of 97) than the scholastic genres do, exactly as one would expect of a text opened and read during a performance rather than shelved. It is spread unusually evenly across the upper north — Phrae 21, Lampang 20, Nan 19, then Chiang Mai 11 and Phayao 10 — with Wat Sung Men far in front at 18 witnesses and Wat Lai Hin Luang second at 7.

And it reaches back further than anything else in the wichaa orbit. 56 of the 97 are dated, running 1541 to 1964 — the oldest being ms 4369, Pali sut hom, from Wat Lai Hin Luang, in monolingual Pali on palm-leaf, 1541. The same title appears at the same temple twice more (ms 4632, ms 4644), also monolingual Pali, undated. Inference — three copies of one Pali-only recitation text kept in one Lampang library, with the earliest dated witness in this genre among them, is what a working choir's music cupboard looks like in the archaeological record: not one revered exemplar, but spare parts.

The saiyasat hinge — why this genre matters to the wichaa

This is the genre where canonical Buddhism and efficacious saiyasat are the same performance seen from two sides. Seven titles here name a thon — the recitation that un-does — and they are the working half of the genre: ms 204 at Wat Phra That Chang Kham (1907) binds the suat boek to the withdrawal for a dead man, for a dead woman, and for all the dead together; ms 363 at Wat Si Mongkhon (1932) does it for the house and the home; ms 521 at Wat Pa Mueat pairs the method of building a house with the sending-off and withdrawal of sappa khuet, all inauspiciousness, and the kalakini of the dwelling. ms 537 at Wat Pa Mueat and ms 2841 at Wat Klang each bind sut mon directly to holasat — the chant and the almanac in one folding book. See thon, which follows this rite across both genres.

The Magic & Ritual article describes the benedictory, consecratory end of saiyasat. This genre is that end, filed under "Chanting" because the technology is a spoken formula and the setting is a vihara full of people. For this archive's esoteric priorities the liturgy is not a backwater — it is where the protective core lives in its most public, communal, and entirely unembarrassed form.

There is one telling asymmetry. Every one of the 388 astrology witnesses and all 276 magic-ritual witnesses are flagged research-priority — but only 6 of these 97 are. Inference — the scorer is reading titles, and a title that says Sut mon looks canonical while a title that says Sainyasat does not. On the evidence of this page, that is the wrong reading of what a sut thon sappakhuet actually does, and re-scoring the liturgy shelf is a live task rather than a hypothetical one.

Notes

  • Read it beside saiyasat, and check for hybrids. The thon sappakhuet, kalakini and sut-mon-with-holasat volumes straddle the liturgy / magic boundary; when a chanting title also names a protective or calendrical element, check the raw metadata — the object is usually a household ritual manual, not pure liturgy.
  • Heavily funerary and occasional. The thon for the dead, the house and misfortune are the practical working half of this genre — the liturgy of the life-cycle. Splitting the paritta and sut from the thon from the suat boek would separate three quite different performance settings and is the obvious next taxonomy pass.
  • The soul-callings are next door, not here. Only one liturgy title names a khwan — ms 367 at Wat Si Mongkhon, Sut lae su khwan cang, chanting bound with the soul-calling of an elephant. The other 32 soul-calling witnesses are filed under magic and ritual; see su khwan and the archive's own living su khwan for machines.
  • Linked to the birth-stories by performance. The invitation to preach the Vessantara — Kam alathana tham wetsantala, ms 370 at Wat Si Mongkhon — ties this genre to jātaka at the Thet Mahachat: the same text is a birth-story on one shelf and a recitation cue on another. ms 673 at Wat Mueang Ram (monolingual Pali, 1893) sets out the fifteen-day cycle "from Yesanta through to the Mahāsamaya Sutta" — a fortnight of chanting written down as an itinerary.
  • Where to go next. Browse the genre to see the 97 in provenance order; the glossary holds the emic vocabulary these titles use; find by need reaches the same rites from the other side, by what a household came wanting.
